slides: Let's continue, and see how the four regions add up to the total.

slides.say: Now the four regions with numbers. A class has thirty students. Twelve play music, fifteen play a sport, and five do both. How many do neither?
Let's put it in the circles. Five do both, so five go in the middle.
at: so five go in the middle

slides.say: Music is twelve, the whole circle. So music only is twelve minus five, seven.
Sport is fifteen. So sport only is fifteen minus five, ten.
Now everyone in at least one circle. Seven plus five plus ten is twenty-two.
There are thirty students. So thirty minus twenty-two, eight do neither.
Now a faster way. A lot of students just add the two groups. Twelve plus fifteen is twenty-seven. But we counted only twenty-two students in the circles. Why the difference?

slides: Because the five in the middle are inside the music circle, and also inside the sport circle. So when we add the two groups, we count them twice.

slides.say: So we subtract them once. Twenty-seven minus five is twenty-two. That's everyone in at least one group.
Then we add the ones outside, neither. So here's the rule. Group A plus group B, minus both, plus neither, is equal to the total.
In our class, twelve plus fifteen, minus five, plus neither, is equal to thirty. So twenty-two plus neither is thirty, and neither is eight. The same eight.
Let's use the rule once more. A club has forty-five members. Twenty-two swim, eighteen play tennis, and ten do both. How many do neither?
Twenty-two plus eighteen is forty. The ten in both were counted twice, so forty minus ten, thirty are in at least one group. So forty-five minus thirty, fifteen do neither.
Why does the rule work? Because now every member is counted exactly once. That's the whole idea. Count each one once.
Let's sum up this lesson. Two groups make four regions. A only, both, B only, and neither. Every member is in exactly one region.
A whole group is its only part plus both. So ten music students means music only plus both.
at: A whole group is its only part

slides.say: Some questions give only a range, and some give an exact answer.
at: Some questions give only a range

slides.say: And to count everyone, we add the two groups, subtract both once, and add neither.

slides: Take a moment to memorize this. Next we'll learn the range questions, the smallest and the biggest overlap. I'll see you in the next video.
